parties:
Sukkur Ali Kha ------ Appellant
Vs.
State ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
11. Before adverting to the arguments pressed into service, the evidences adduced from the prosecution side may be discussed in brief. 

 12. PW 1 is the Sub-Inspector of Police who lodged the First Information Report. He gave testimony that in the matter of execution of a warrant of arrest against accused Sukkur Ali, he on 27-8-94 along with police personnel’s, went to village Charbaria under Kotwali Police Station and ongoing there he got the information that the accused Sukkur Ali was residing in village Gilatali with his family. He then being accompanied by PW 6 Khondkar Wares, PW 5 Motahar Hossain Chowdhury and PW 4 Shajahan Negaban on 28-8-94 at 6-30 AM went to the house of the accused Sukkur Ali at Village-Gilatali and called him. The accused opened the door after several calls. He went inside the house and secured the arrest of the accused and on searching his body recovered one bayonet of 303 Rifle, measuring 22" in presence of witnesses and prepared a seizure list. In cross-examination he stated that the accused after many calls opened the door of the hut. He further stated that he entered into the but when the accused opened the door of the house. He also gave evidence that the villagers of Gilatali Village were not cited as witnesses in the case. This witness further testified that in the seizure list there was no mention wherefrom the arms had been recovered. He denied the suggestion that no arms had been recovered from the possession of the accused and he was implicated falsely. 

 14. PW 3 is 29 Battallion Md Haroon Molla, a member of BDR. This witness gave evidence that on going to the village Gilatali the house of accused Sukkur Ali was gheraoed and Daroga Ali Hassan brought out the accused from the house and on searching his body a bayonet of 303 rifle was found. In cross-examination this witness testified that after repeated calls the door of the house was opened and the Daroga on entering into the house arrested the accused who thereafter,was brought to the verandha of the house and on searching his body, a bayonet was recovered from his possession and control. This witness further gave evidence that at the time of search, no person was present at the spot and persons came after the search. 

 16. PW 5 is Mothahar Hossain Chowdhury, an inhabitant of village Char Hogla under Police Station Kotwali. This witness in his evidence stated that he met the police force at the local Chader Hat and Daroga was previously known to him. Daroga after preparation of the seizure list took his signature on it. He further stated that in his presence Union Parishad Member Wares Khondker put his signature on the seizure list. In cross-examination this witness stated that in his presence no arms had been recovered from the possession of the accused or from the house of the accused. This witness gave further testimony that arms shown to him at Chader Hat was not produced in the Court. 

 17. PW 6 is Khondker Wares who is a resident of village Pashurkhali and also a Union Parishad Member. This witness in his evidence stated that he saw at Chader Hat Sub-Inspector of Police Ali Hasan and 3/4 police personnels. This witness further stated that at the Bazar he heard that a dagger was recovered from the possession of the accused and the police had shown that dagger to him. He further testified that at the dictation of the police, he signed on a written paper. In cross-examination this witness stated that in his presence no arms had been recovered. He again stated that he did not put signature on the written paper on reading the same and as a Union Parishad Member, he on bonafide faith, put signature on the seizure list. 

 19. Having regard to the evidence adduced by the prosecution in support of its case we now propose to deal with the first branch of argument advanced on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution signally failed to prove the recovery of arms ie bayonet from the possession of the appellant and an order of acquittal was required to be passed upon him. 

 26. It can hardly be disputed that it is for the prosecution to prove "possession" strictly in order to sustain a conviction under section 19 (f) of the Arms Act. If there is any doubt as to "possession", the accused must be given the benefit of it. It is well recognized that a conviction under section 19(f) of the Arms Act cannot be allowed to stand unless the prosecution has adduced sufficient evidence to testify that the accused person has in his "possession" or under his "control" arms and ammunition in contravention of sections 4, 14, 15 and 19 of the said Act. 

 27. The real question that falls for determination in this appeal is whether the accused appellant was in "possession" of the incriminating article ie the bayonet or not. PW 1 the Informant Sub-Inspector of Police stated that after many calls accused appellant opened the door of the but and he on entering into the house arrested the appellant and recovered the arms from the waist of his body inside a lungi in presence of the witnesses and prepared seizure list wherein the witnesses put their signatures. PW 2 the constable who accompanied PW 1 to the house of the appellant in his evidence stated that the accused after repeated calls opened the door and PW 1 on entering into the house brought out the appellant from inside the house and on the courtyard searched him and found the bayonet hidden on his waist under the lungi. PW 2 also stated that seizure list was prepared in presence of the persons who were present on the spot and those persons put their signatures on the seizure list. PW 3 gave testimony that there had been calls for a pretty long time and thereafter, the door was opened and PW 1 entered into the house and secured the arrest of the accused. It was his further statement that the accused was dragged to the verandah of the house and on searching his body the bayonet was recovered from his "possession" and "control". PW 3 also stated that at the time of search nobody had been present and people came later on. PWs 4, 5 and 6, the alleged witnesses of the recovery and seizure of the bayonet and witnesses of the seizure list, categorically stated that no arms had been recovered from the "possession" of the accused in their presence and they do not know anything of the recovery and under the dictation of PW 1, they put signatures on the seizure list at Chader Hat Bazar. PW 7 is the Investigating Officer who stated that he did not examine any person of the places mentioned in the sketch map and also did not examine any person of village Gilatali. 

 28. On a close analysis of the prosecution evidences, it appears that the witnesses as to the recovery of the arms ie bayonet from the "possession" of the accused appellant and the place and manner of recovery suffers from glaring contradictions, inconsistencies and infirmities and it is difficult to believe the prosecution case as to the recovery of the bayonet from the "possession" or "control" of the appellant. The existence of mens rea or guilty knowledge on the part of the accused appellant could not be also established by the prosecution. The prosecution thus appears to have failed to bring home the charge against the accused appellant beyond all reasonable doubt. The first branch of argument appears to have a good deal of force. 

 29. Another vital aspect of the matter must not be overlooked. The prosecution case has been grounded on the fact that after repeated calls the accused-appellant opened the door and on searching his body, whether inside the house, or on the courtyard or on the verandah, the bayonet was recovered from his body hidden on his waist under the lungi. Now the question is: Can it be at all believable that hearing many calls from outside by police personnel’s and other people for opening the door of the house, the accused-appellant opened the door keeping the bayonet on his waist under the lungi to have the same recovered from his body. The answer is: It is impossible and also improbable. It is the evidence that the accused-appellant did not open the door of the house at the first call but opened the same after repeated calls. The appellant, before opening the door of the house, took much time to hide the bayonet in any place of the house. The appellant''s first anxiety would have been to keep the bayonet in a hidden place when the house was alleged to be of a dacoit. The prosecution version of the case, therefore, suffers from an inherent improbability and also an infirmity of a serious nature. 

 30. Let us now turn to the second branch of argument pressed into service on behalf of the accused appellant that the search of the body of the accused-appellant and seizure of the bayonet having not at all been proved in accordance with law, the conviction and sentence upon the accused-appellant cannot be sustained in law. Referring to section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure it was attempted to be argued that in the matter of search and seizure of arms ie bayonet, the provisions of law contained in section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was not all complied with and since the search and the seizure had not been conducted in presence of two respectable inhabitants of the locality, the conviction and sentence upon the accused-appellant cannot be allowed to stand at all. 

 31. Referring to section 51 of the Code of Criminal Procedure it was submitted from the side of the State that the arrest of the accused-appellant having been made in execution of warrant of arrest in connection with a dacoit case, the provision contained in section 103 of the Code was not at all attracted, rather section 51 of the Code was applicable in the present case and under the provision of section 51 of the Code, the police was authorized to search the accused-appellant after his arrest. 

 32. For the purpose of answering to the point so raised it will be useful to notice both sections 103 and 51 of the Code of Criminal Procedure which are quoted as such: 

 Section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: 

 "103-(1) Before making a search under this Chapter, the officer or other person about to make it shall call upon two or more respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situate to attend and witness the search and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do. 

 33. A combined reading of sub-sections 1 and 2 of section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure reveals that the search of a place and seizure of things by the police must be conducted in the presence of two or more respectable inhabitants of the locality. Section 103 of the Code appears under Chapter-VII. 

 35. It is, thus, evidently clear that section 103 of the Code relates to the search of a place by the police officer and got no manner of application in respect of a search of an arrested person by a police officer. It is in the First Information Report and also in the evidence that in execution of a warrant of arrest in GR Case No. 88 of 1992 the police went to the house of the accused-appellant to secure his arrest and after arrest search was conducted upon him. So the search of the body of the accused appellant was very much sanctioned by law under section 51 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The second branch of argument advanced from the side of the appellant is devoid of any substance.
